CASE REPORT
Neonatal Hyperekplexia (The Stiff Baby Syndrome)
MUHAMMAD SAEED, HISHAM AL-DHALAAN, AHMAD WALI, Waheed Ahmad
Sixteen days old baby was referred to our pediatric neurology OPD for evaluation.
Sixteen days old baby was referred to our pediatric neurology OPD for evaluation.

Mother was primigravida with no significant medical or surgical history. Baby was admitted in nursery at Children Hospital Taif, because of limited joint movement and generalized stiffness of all the four limbs.

Baby was admitted in nursery at Children Hospital Taif, because of limited joint movement and generalized stiffness of all the four limbs. On second day of admission doctor on duty in nursery noticed generalized increased tone of the body during examination and exaggerated startle reaction to noise and tactile stimuli. Moreover, there was no history of swallowing difficulty, or any abnormal movement or seizures. On examination, she had normal vital signs. No dysmorphism or neurocutaneous stigmata with normal red eye reflex in both eyes. CNS examination revealed increased tone in all muscle groups of the body and in abdominal muscles as well. During examination she held herself in flexed posture, with clenching of hands. Her deep tendon reflexes were normal. We elicited increase startle response by tapping the nasal bridge and foot during examination.

Diagnosis of hereditary Hyperekplexia requires the following three cardinal features:
1. Generalized stiffness immediately after birth.
2. Excessive startle response.
3. Generalized stiffness followed by startle response

Diagnosis is usually made clinically; electromyography test shows continuous electrical activity at rest with decreased latencies.

The best treatment of choice for Hyperekplexia mentioned in the literature is with clonazepam. Clonzaepam increases GABA-gated chloride channel function and compensate for the defective glycine-gated chloride channel in Hyperekplexia. Therapeutic response to clonazepam is dramatic enough to be diagnostic.
